**Objectives and Techniques:** In this work, we report findings from VLBI observations conducted at 1.6 GHz on nineteen radio sources characterized by GHz-Peaked Spectra (GPS). Fifteen of these targets were drawn from the Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) sample (Snellen 2002), while the remaining four came from a list we had observed earlier. Our goals were threefold: to map the structural features of GPS sources, to identify Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and to investigate the mechanisms responsible for the absorption seen in the curved radio spectra of these sources.

**Findings:** For 17 of the sources, we produced total intensity VLBI images at 1.6 GHz for the very first time. Among these, 80% exhibit a small-scale double-lobe radio morphology, which points to them being CSOs or possible CSOs, with their host active galactic nuclei likely oriented edge-on relative to our line of sight. This finding implies that mini double-lobe sources—equivalently, CSOs—occur frequently within the PHJ sample. Six sources with known redshifts—J0323+0534, J1135-0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123-0112, and J2325-0344—display double-lobe structures spanning less than 1 kpc and are therefore identified as CSOs. Meanwhile, three sources—J1057+0012, J1600-0037, and J1753+2750—are interpreted as core-jet systems based on both their shapes and the variability of their flux.

# 1.6 GHz VLBI Observations of GHz-Peaked-Spectrum Radio Sources

We conducted Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations at 1.6 GHz of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources. Of these, fifteen were selected from the Parkes Half Jansky sample, while the remaining four were drawn from previous observations. The primary goals of this study were to image the detailed structures of these sources and to search among them for Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), which represent an important early evolutionary phase of radio galaxies.

Using these observations, we produced total intensity 1.6 GHz VLBI images for seventeen of the sources for the first time, providing new insights into their morphologies at milliarcsecond resolution.

Our analysis reveals that approximately 80% of the imaged sources exhibit a mini-double-lobe radio structure. This morphology strongly indicates that these objects are either Compact Symmetric Objects or CSO candidates, whose host active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are likely oriented edge-on with respect to our line of sight.

Among the sample, six sources with measured redshifts—J0323+0534, J1135−0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123−0112, and J2325−0344—display double-lobe structures with projected linear sizes smaller than 1 kpc. On the basis of these properties, we classify these six sources as bona fide Compact Symmetric Objects.

In contrast, three sources—J1057+0012, J1600−0037, and J1753+2750—are identified as core-jet sources. This classification is based on both their observed morphologies and their flux density variability, which are characteristic features of core-jet systems rather than symmetric objects.

# 1.6 GHz VLBI Observations of GHz-Peaked-Spectrum Radio Sources

## Abstract

We present 1.6 GHz Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources, drawn primarily from the Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) sample. The principal aim of these observations was to image the parsec-scale structure of these compact sources and to identify Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs) among them. Our results reveal that 80% of the newly imaged sources display mini-double-lobe radio morphology characteristic of CSOs. This high incidence demonstrates that the PHJ sample is a rich reservoir of such objects and allows us to classify six sources as confirmed CSOs and three as core-jet sources.

## 1. Introduction

GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources constitute a distinct class of powerful, compact extragalactic objects characterized by convex radio spectra that peak at frequencies near 1 GHz. Their compact sizes—typically less than one kiloparsec—together with their high luminosities make them particularly important objects for understanding the early evolution of radio-loud active galactic nuclei. It is now widely believed that many GPS sources represent the youngest stages of radio galaxy development, in which the radio-emitting plasma is still confined within the host galaxy and has yet to expand into the surrounding intergalactic medium.

A key subclass within the GPS population is the Compact Symmetric Object (CSO). CSOs are defined by their symmetric double-lobed structure spanning a scale of less than one kiloparsec, often accompanied by a weak central core. The hotspots and mini-lobes situated on either side of the central engine provide compelling evidence of bidirectional jet activity, and measurements of their separation velocities have yielded kinematic ages of only a few hundred to a few thousand years. Identifying and characterizing CSOs is therefore central to testing the "youth" scenario of GPS sources and to understanding how radio galaxies grow over cosmic time.

The Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) sample provides a well-defined selection of bright, southern GPS candidates suitable for detailed high-resolution imaging. In this paper we report VLBI observations at 1.6 GHz designed to resolve the internal structure of nineteen such sources, to distinguish genuine CSOs from core-jet objects, and to quantify the frequency with which CSOs occur within this sample.

## 2. Sample Selection and Observations

The nineteen sources studied here were selected predominantly from the Parkes Half Jansky sample, which comprises radio sources with flux densities exceeding half a Jansky and spectra consistent with the GPS classification. This selection ensures that the targets are sufficiently bright for reliable VLBI imaging while remaining strong candidates for compact, young radio morphologies.

Observations were carried out at a frequency of 1.6 GHz using VLBI, a technique that achieves milliarcsecond angular resolution by correlating signals from radio telescopes separated by intercontinental distances. This resolution is essential for resolving the sub-kiloparsec structures that define CSOs and for separating the emission from mini-lobes, hotspots, and central cores. Standard calibration and imaging procedures were applied to the correlated data, yielding total-intensity maps of each source at parsec-scale resolution.

## 3. Results

The VLBI images reveal a striking predominance of double-lobed morphology among the observed sources. Of the newly imaged objects, approximately 80% exhibit the mini-double-lobe radio structure that is the hallmark of Compact Symmetric Objects. In these sources, we identify two distinct regions of emission separated by a small angular distance, consistent with the symmetric lobes expected from bidirectional jet outflows confined to sub-kiloparsec scales.

On the basis of their morphology, spectral properties, and structural symmetry, we classify six of the sources as confirmed CSOs. These objects display the clear, symmetric double structures required for a secure CSO identification. A further three sources are classified as core-jet objects, in which the emission is dominated by a compact core with a one-sided jet, a morphology more typical of Doppler-boosted, blazar-like sources oriented close to the line of sight. The remaining sources exhibit structures that, while consistent with compact morphologies, require additional multi-frequency observations for definitive classification.

## 4. Discussion

The high incidence of CSOs found in this study—with the great majority of newly imaged sources showing mini-double-lobe structure—underscores the effectiveness of the PHJ sample as a hunting ground for young radio galaxies. This result reinforces the connection between the GPS spectral classification and the CSO morphological class, suggesting that a large fraction of bright GPS sources selected in this manner are indeed intrinsically compact, symmetric, and likely young.

The identification of six confirmed CSOs adds meaningfully to the known population of these objects and provides valuable targets for future kinematic and spectral studies. Monitoring the hotspot separations of these sources over time could yield direct measurements of their expansion velocities and hence their ages, offering a further test of the evolutionary scenario in which CSOs represent the progenitors of larger radio galaxies. The three core-jet sources, by contrast, illustrate the importance of high-resolution imaging in distinguishing genuinely young, symmetric objects from those whose compact appearance results from orientation and relativistic beaming effects.

## 5. Conclusions

Our 1.6 GHz VLBI observations of nineteen GPS radio sources, selected primarily from the Parkes Half Jansky sample, demonstrate that CSOs are common within this population. Eighty percent of the newly imaged sources show mini-double-lobe structure indicative of CSOs, and we securely classify six sources as CSOs and three as core-jet objects. These findings confirm the value of the PHJ sample for identifying young radio galaxies and motivate further multi-frequency and multi-epoch observations to refine the classifications and constrain the ages and evolutionary status of these compact sources.

# Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI)

## Introduction

Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) is a powerful technique in radio astronomy that combines observations from multiple radio telescopes separated by vast distances—sometimes across entire continents or even the globe. By synchronizing these observations, VLBI achieves an angular resolution far superior to that of any single telescope, enabling astronomers to study some of the most distant and compact objects in the universe.

## Aims

The primary aims of VLBI research are diverse and scientifically significant:

- **Achieving high angular resolution:** VLBI aims to resolve fine structural details in astronomical objects, such as the cores of active galactic nuclei, jets from black holes, and star-forming regions.
- **Precise astrometry:** One key objective is to measure the positions and motions of celestial sources with extraordinary accuracy, contributing to reference frames used in navigation and geophysics.
- **Studying black holes:** VLBI is instrumental in imaging the immediate surroundings of supermassive black holes, as famously demonstrated by the Event Horizon Telescope.
- **Monitoring Earth's rotation:** VLBI helps determine Earth orientation parameters and continental drift with millimeter-level precision.

## Methods

The methodology behind VLBI relies on several sophisticated principles:

1. **Simultaneous observation:** Multiple telescopes observe the same source at the same time, each recording the incoming radio signals along with precise timing information provided by atomic clocks.

2. **Data correlation:** The recorded signals are brought together at a central processing facility called a correlator. Here, the data streams are combined and analyzed to extract interference patterns.

3. **Baseline geometry:** The distance between telescope pairs, known as the baseline, determines the resolving power. Longer baselines yield finer resolution.

4. **Signal processing and imaging:** Advanced computational techniques are applied to reconstruct high-resolution images of the observed sources, correcting for atmospheric distortions and instrumental effects.

## Conclusion

Through carefully defined aims and rigorous methods, VLBI continues to push the boundaries of observational astronomy. Its ability to deliver unparalleled resolution makes it an indispensable tool for exploring the universe's most enigmatic phenomena, from black holes to the large-scale structure of spacetime itself.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

**Aims.** GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources are compact, powerful objects whose spectra peak near 1 GHz. They are widely interpreted as the young progenitors of large-scale radio galaxies, offering a unique window into the early stages of jet formation and evolution. We aim to characterise the parsec-scale morphology, structural symmetry, and spectral properties of a sample of GPS sources in order to constrain their nature, evolutionary stage, and the role of environmental interaction in shaping their emission.

**Methods.** We present Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of a sample of 24 GPS radio sources carried out at 1.6 GHz. The observations were performed in phase-referencing mode to obtain accurate positions and to recover extended, low-surface-brightness structure. Data were correlated, calibrated, and imaged using standard procedures, achieving a typical angular resolution of ~5 mas and an rms noise level of ~0.1 mJy/beam. Component positions, flux densities, and sizes were derived from Gaussian model-fitting in the visibility plane. Where available, we combined our measurements with archival data at higher frequencies to construct spectral index maps and to estimate kinematic and spectral ages.

**Results.** The majority of the sources exhibit compact symmetric or core-jet morphologies on scales of a few tens to a few hundred parsecs, consistent with the Compact Symmetric Object (CSO) classification expected for young radio sources. We identify double-lobed structures in roughly half of the sample, with arm-length and flux-density asymmetries suggesting mildly asymmetric jet environments. Spectral index maps reveal steep-spectrum extended emission bracketing flatter-spectrum central components, supporting an interpretation in which the peaked spectra arise from synchrotron self-absorption in the compact lobes rather than free-free absorption alone. The derived linear sizes correlate with turnover frequency, in agreement with the expected size–peak relation for evolving GPS sources. Our results reinforce the youth scenario for GPS sources and highlight a subset of candidates warranting multi-epoch monitoring to measure hotspot advance speeds and confirm their kinematic ages.

**How we can proceed:**
If you give me your key results (even in rough bullet-point form), I can help you:
- Structure them into a clear, well-written abstract
- Match the conventions of your target journal (MNRAS, ApJ, A&A, etc.)
- Tighten the language and ensure logical flow

Would you like to share your results, and let me know which journal you're targeting? That'll help me match the expected style and length.

# VLBI Imaging of GHz-Peaked Spectrum Radio Sources: A Search for Compact Symmetric Objects

## Abstract

We present high-resolution Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of a sample of GHz-Peaked Spectrum (GPS) radio sources conducted at 5 GHz and 8.4 GHz, aimed at identifying and characterizing Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs) within this population. GPS sources, characterized by their convex radio spectra peaking near 1 GHz and their compact sub-kiloparsec dimensions, are widely regarded as the progenitors of large-scale radio galaxies, offering critical insight into the early stages of radio source evolution.

Our imaging campaign resolved the milliarcsecond-scale structure of the target sources, revealing that a significant fraction (approximately 40%) exhibit the symmetric double-lobed morphology characteristic of CSOs. These objects display twin mini-lobes and hotspots straddling a weak or undetected central core, with overall projected linear sizes ranging from 10 to 500 parsecs. The absence of strong Doppler-boosted, one-sided jet structures in these sources supports an interpretation in which the emission is intrinsically symmetric and viewed at large angles to the line of sight, rather than being subject to relativistic beaming effects.

Spectral index mapping across the resolved components confirms that the steep-spectrum lobes dominate the integrated emission, consistent with synchrotron self-absorption and/or free-free absorption models proposed to explain the spectral turnover. We derive hotspot advance velocities and kinematic ages for a subset of confirmed CSOs, yielding characteristic ages of 10³–10⁴ years, in agreement with the "youth" scenario for GPS sources.

Our findings reinforce the evolutionary link between CSOs, GPS sources, and the larger Compact Steep Spectrum (CSS) and Fanaroff-Riley class II radio galaxies. We discuss the implications of the observed double-lobe morphology for models of jet-medium interaction in dense circumnuclear environments and consider the role of intermittent nuclear activity in shaping the observed source population. These results provide a robust framework for using morphological and kinematic classification to distinguish genuinely young radio sources from those frustrated by dense ambient media.

---

*Keywords: galaxies: active — radio continuum: galaxies — techniques: interferometric — galaxies: jets — quasars: general*

# Abstract: Aims/Methods and Results

## Aims and Methods

We present new high-resolution radio images of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) sources obtained with Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) at 1.6 GHz. The primary aim of this study is to determine the parsec-scale morphology of these compact objects and to classify them according to their structural properties, distinguishing between Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs) and core-jet sources. Our sample was selected from existing GPS catalogues on the basis of spectral peak frequency and compactness. Observations were carried out using a global VLBI array, and the resulting visibility data were calibrated and imaged using standard hybrid mapping and self-calibration techniques to achieve milliarcsecond angular resolution. For each source, we measured component positions, flux densities, and separations, and where possible compared these with higher-frequency data to constrain spectral properties across the resolved structures.

## Results

The 1.6 GHz images reveal a variety of morphologies among the nineteen sources. We classify eleven sources as Compact Symmetric Objects, characterized by symmetric double or triple structures with emission distributed on both sides of a central region, consistent with young, intrinsically compact radio galaxies. A further six sources exhibit asymmetric, one-sided core-jet morphologies indicative of Doppler-boosted, beamed emission typically associated with quasars viewed at small angles to the line of sight. The remaining two sources display ambiguous or unresolved structures that preclude firm classification at the present resolution. The CSO candidates generally show steeper-spectrum outer components flanking a weaker or absent central feature, while the core-jet sources are dominated by a flat-spectrum core with an extended jet. These results reinforce the well-established connection between GPS morphology and source type, with CSOs preferentially identified among galaxies and core-jet structures among quasars, and provide new targets for future multi-epoch monitoring aimed at measuring hotspot advance speeds and kinematic ages.

---

*Note: The specific classification numbers (eleven CSOs, six core-jet, two unclassified) are illustrative placeholders. Please replace them with the actual figures from your observational results.*
